91. Outer Limits! 限る & 限り: 
Its many meanings and how they work 
知っている限り、とは限らない and more
Outer Limits! 限る Kagiru 限り Kagiri - Its many meanings and how they work 知っている限り、とは限らない and more
こんにちは。
Today we're going to talk about "限る" and "限り".
"限る" is a verb meaning "limit" or "restrict",
and "限り" is the い-stem, therefore the noun-form of that verb.
【図】Red 限る labelled LIMIT and blue 限り labelled THE OUTER, both sitting above a brown picket fence. No arrows; the English labels sit beside their words.
If you don't know about い-stems making noun-forms,

I'll link a video above my head which tells you all the secrets of the mysterious い-stem.
(Lesson 72)
Now, Japanese likes limiting expressions, expressions to do with limits and boundaries.

I did a video on "うち" (Lesson 97) a little while ago 
and I'll put a link above my head and in the information section below.
"うち" concentrates on the enclosure, on the area that we're in
and everything else is outside of.
"限り", on the other hand, concentrates on the boundaries of that enclosure,
the edges beyond which the enclosure does not reach.
And this gives rise to a whole range of expression strategies,
some of which are quite literal, others of which are very metaphorical
and can confuse people if they don't understand where they're coming from.
限る
So, let's start with a very simple use of "限る".
"出席は招待者に限る"
"出席" is attendance at whatever the event may be.
It is limited at "招待者" (invited persons).
Outside that limit, "出席" doesn't exist.
You can't attend the meeting or whatever unless you are an invited person.

【図】Title 出席は招待者に限る with 限る in red above a red carpet flanked by six stanchions whose ropes connect the posts on each side; an easel sign reads 出席は 招待者に限る. No arrows; the roped carpet depicts an exclusive entrance, glossed "attendance is limited to invited guests."
Now, another mainly literal use is "声の限りに呼んだ" (I called at the limit of my voice).
In English we might say "the top of my voice".
【図】Cartoon calico cat with an orange bow tie standing on hind legs, one paw raised, mouth open with motion lines. Headline in blue and red reads 声の限りに呼んだ. No diagram labels or arrows.
What we're saying here is the limit as loud as my voice would go.
So these are quite literal and easy to understand.
But then we get expressions which I think most of you will have heard
at some time and are perhaps a little more confusing.
So, "夏はアイスクリイムに限る" -- now, loosely in English that means
"In summer, ice cream is the best thing".
【図】Summer cartoon scene: cicada on a tree, smiling sun, boy with a blue paddle fan and girl holding ice cream on a green mound. Main sentence 夏はアイスクリームに限る; no diagram labels or arrows.

What we're actually saying is 
"Speaking of summer, when it comes to summer, it reaches its limit at ice cream",
in other words, ice cream is the furthest you can take summer /

ice cream is the pinnacle of summer / 
there's nothing beyond ice cream when we're talking about summer.
Note: Of course, this is just a natural Eng translation, hence why it is hard to pin-point 限る here.
And this can be used in all kinds of different expressions, for example:

"運動なら水泳に限る" 
(if it's exercise / if we're talking about exercise, it reaches its limit with swimming ["水泳"] /
swimming is absolutely the best kind of exercise).
【図】Cartoon of a child in a blue swim cap swimming freestyle in blue water, bubbles and splashes around. Caption at the bottom: 運動なら水泳に限る, with 限る in red. No labels or arrows.
And moving on from this we get expressions like "彼女に限ってそんなことはしない".
【図】Slide shows the sentence 彼女に限ってそんなことはしない, with 限って in red and the rest in blue, beside a chibi angel girl with halo and blue wings. No diagram labels or arrows.

And again, in loose English this would be 
"She of all people wouldn't do such a thing
/ she'd be the last person to do such a thing".
What we're actually saying is
"She is the very limit of people who wouldn't do such a thing".

So just like ice cream being the best thing in summer 
or calling at the very maximum extent of your voice, 
she is the maximum, the extreme of people who wouldn't do such a thing.
Other people might possibly do it, even if you'd think they wouldn't,
but she is the very limit of the kind of person who wouldn't do that kind of thing.
限る used negatively (not limited to x)
Now, the concept of "限る" (limit) is often used negatively to show that
something is not limited to a particular statement, a particular notion.
So, "辞書に書いてあることが常に正しいとは限らない".
【図】Anime-style girl with black hair and red glasses reading an open book while touching her temple, above the sentence 辞書に書いてあることが、常に正しいとは限らない。 with 限らない in red. No diagram labels or arrows.
And this "-とは限らない" essentially sums up the previous statement
and says that's not limited to being the case.
So what we're saying here is "Things that are written in a dictionary are always correct" --
that's the statement, then we quote that "-とは限らない":
"It's not necessarily the case that things written in a dictionary are always correct."
And I think we found that out to be true on various occasions.
限り
Now, again, this "限り" can be used for the limits of one's knowledge and very often is,
so "私の知っている限りではそんな言葉はない".

【図】White cartoon rabbit with pink inner ears and cheeks raising a paw beside a large red question mark. Text 私の知っている限りでは そんな言葉はない, with 限り in red, meaning "as far as I know, there is no such word." No arrows.

So, in English we would say "As far as I know, there's no such word", 
but the expression strategy here is to modify the noun "限り" -- "私の知っている限り"
(the limit of what I know): "Up to the limit of what I know, there is no such word."
And actually in this case it's pretty similar to the English:
"as far as I know / to the limit of what I know".
And it's interesting here that while English says "as far as I know",
Japanese achieves the same broad pattern by modifying the noun "限り" (limit).

And as we talked about last week (Lesson 90), 
modification does an awful lot of the heavy lifting in Japanese
that's done by other strategies in English.
Now, another common expression which can be a bit confusing is the kind of expression
we find in "急いでいる時に限ってバスが遅れる"
(limited to times when we are in a hurry, the bus comes late).

【図】Slide with the sentence 急いでいる時に限ってバスが遅れる, 限 highlighted red. An annoyed schoolgirl in a blue blazer waits at a bus shelter with smartphone and drink, next to a bus-stop sign and timetable, in front of a cosmetics poster with a blonde model. No diagram labels or arrows.
Now, this is obviously not literal, but it expresses a sentiment often felt,
that the bus or whatever it is that does something we don't want it to do does it
specifically when we very much don't want or can't afford it to do it.
So really that expression that can seem a little bit confusing at first is a very natural
kind of expression which I think you do find in English sometimes.
It's only when we really need it that it doesn't happen.
その場限り
Now, another expression is "その場限り".

So, "その場限りことを言う" means 
she says things on the spur of the moment / she talks right off the top of her head.

【図】Slide shows その場限りのことを言う, with 場限り in red and the rest blue, above a smiling woman in a red cap and uniform raising her index finger. It illustrates saying something only for that occasion; no diagram labels or arrows.
"その場", which we've discussed in another video, which I'll link (Lesson 75), means literally
"that place / the appropriate place / the place one would happen to be at at the time", but
of course in Japanese as in other languages, place can also mean a time or an occasion.

So, "その場限りことを言う" means 
she says things that just arise out of the particular occasion and nothing else -- 
limited to that particular occasion / having no real relevance outside that particular occasion.
So the implication is just essentially talking stuff of no real value that
comes off the top of her head.
その場限りさ
And a very common expression related to this is "喧嘩はその場限りさ" – ケンカ
and this is a popular expression, it's not exactly a full sentence.

【図】Title in blue and red reads ケンカはその場限りさ above two angry children — a boy in a pink shirt and green shorts at left and a girl in a blue floral dress at right, each with clenched fists and a grey anger puff whose tail points at them. No other labels.
Note: I used Kanji form for ケンカ (喧嘩), but both are fine.
The "さ" is rather making it into a "should".
"さ" here is saying "that's how it ought to be / come on, that's how it should be".
And it's translated into English as "quarrels should not be continued".

【図】Dark-mode YouTube comment thread under a Japanese lesson: @liniou asks "さ can mean should?" and @organicjapanesewithcuredol49 replies "Not really, but it can be a sort of gee-up expression." Only comment/reply UI and a blue reply-thread triangle beside "2 replies"; no labels or arrows.
Sometimes it's even translated as "let not the sun settle on your wrath",
which of course is nothing to do with what it's really saying.
But the point here is that quarrels should be limited to "その場"
(the occasion, the event on which they arise).
So if you quarrel with someone today you shouldn't be carrying on that quarrel tomorrow.
Very good advice.
So this is a range of the circumstances in which the "限り / 限る" concept
is applied in Japanese.

【図】Slide shows a brown picket fence across the bottom with two glossy Japanese forms: red 限る at upper left with the black diagonal label “LIMIT,” and blue 限り at lower right with the black diagonal label “THE OUTER.” No arrows; labels sit near their forms, with the fence representing an outer boundary.
There are others, of course, but with this information
I think you'll be in a better position to see what's going on.

【図】Screenshot of a YouTube comment thread, not a teaching slide: @theblackryvius6613 asks the difference between "this" and ほど, and @organicjapanesewithcuredol49 replies that they are not interchangeable and links a ほど video. The commenter contrasts ほど ("to the extent of") with 限り ("to the limit of"). No diagrams.

【図】Screenshot of three YouTube comments arguing that usage and purpose matter more than rigid rules and that natural expression comes from immersion rather than memorised rules. No Japanese text, diagrams or arrows.

【図】Dark-mode YouTube comment thread: @theblackryvius6613 says they rarely see words like わけ and suggests a video on fossils in Modern Japanese such as 思いきや; Cure Dolly replies with a link to https://youtu.be/iU79wvDyDfk (2 years ago). No diagram.

Note: The links referred are くらい vs ほど and Lesson 68 for わけ. You can check other comments under the video as usual. 
Anyway, this is where Dolly’s Grammar playlist of 93 videos officially ends. We are reaching the end. There are a few other converted videos by Dolly below this yet.
